chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.html:
“I’ve located them. The admin logs on NeiKos496…on Phainon.”

He should be interested, but it’s all a dull roaring in his ears. The turmoil within him distracts him from much else.

“Intra-Cognition is null. Responds only to destructive stimuli.”

The sentence barely registers in Mydei’s mind as his eyes remain fixed on the shadow of the man who was once Phainon, who sits completely still in a chair, staring sightlessly ahead.

“Damage to mind function detected… Possibly irreversible…”

The Antikytheran-like man continues reading through the digitized logs impartially, as if merely reciting a speech. But every single word he says drives another stake into Mydei’s heart.

He can gather bits and pieces of what had happened, beyond the complicated outworld jargon. Mydei had died. All of the Chrysos Heirs had perished, giving their lives to pave the way for Deliverance. But the truth behind Amphoreus’ ill fate had been far crueler than any one of them could even imagine, the product of a lab experiment dressed up as an epic that was doomed from the very beginning.

In the end, to defy that fate, Phainon had willingly walked towards his own Destruction, all to ruin Lygus’ plans and give the world and the people in it a single chance at life.

Perhaps he would have been able to retain some semblance of himself had he simply perished as he had hoped and was restored alongside everyone else. But the forceful merging with the thing called Irontomb had destroyed what had been left of his fraying sanity. Defiant until the very end, Phainon had fought ferociously from within the Lord Ravager itself, buying enough time for the revived Chrysos Heirs and the Trailblazers to terminate its birth for good—

—but the immense effort he had expended to do so had been the final nail in the coffin on his already-damaged mind and body, leaving him in this near-vegetative state.

“It’s a miracle that we were able to restore him at all,” Mydei hears the Antikytheran man remark quietly to the Astral Express members, several of whom he does not recognize. The ones he does know, Stelle and Dan Heng, lower their heads, their expressions torn by remorse. “But as for whether we can restore his mind… While Madam Herta may argue that nothing is impossible for the Genius Society, I would advise you not to raise your hopes too high.

“33,550,336 cycles over hundreds of Amber Eras… It is difficult to fathom the insanity that this man has had to endure. Perhaps his sole saving grace was his nature as a data entity created from memoria—any normal organic being would have been destroyed in a fraction of the time.”

The conversation fades to background noise after that. Perhaps he should continue listening—it concerns his beloved, after all—but just this once, he is unable to muster an ounce of his indominable will to persevere. Not when he’s forced to hear about the cruelty and unjustness of it all.

Phainon was one of the three who fought for Amphoreus’ first true dawn. So why is it that he is the only one unable to witness it?

What point is there to a dawn without the sun?

“Mydei.”

A voice jerks Mydei out of his morose thoughts and he turns to see Dan Heng approaching. Beside him is another young man who appears to be around the same age, with shoulder-length grey hair, amber eyes, and, more peculiarly, a pair of wings sprouting from behind his ears and a metallic-looking halo floating behind his head. An older gentleman with brown hair and glasses accompanies them both, though an odd look enters his eyes the moment he sees Phainon. Mydei isn’t sure whether he likes the way he stares at him, but he holds his tongue. If they’re here to help, then he’ll be civil.

It’s Dan Heng who speaks first, introducing his companions. “These two are Sunday and Welt Yang, fellow Nameless who are traveling on the Astral Express. We were wondering if you were okay with us taking a look at Phainon.”

“Can you help him?” Mydei asks a little too quickly.

“We can’t make any promises,” the bespectacled gentleman, Welt Yang, replies. “But getting a better idea of his current state might guide us in the right direction.”

“Then, by all means.”

He steps aside, glancing down at Dan Heng and noticing the distinct lack of a second person by his side. “Where did Stelle go?”

“She left to brainstorm some ideas with March, Cyrene, and Black Swan,” Dan Heng replies. “They're trying to come up with a way to restore memory, since that might help bring him out of his state, but…we’re not sure if anything will work on Phainon just yet. His case seems to be very complex.”

Mydei tries not to let that shake him too much, instead turning to the other two. They’re discussing Phainon’s condition quietly, but their conversation is still audible from where he and Dan Heng are standing.

“Were you able to find anything, Mr. Sunday?”

The wing-headed boy, Sunday, shakes his head. “From what I can tell, there have been only a few instances of external interference, most of them stemming from the Lord Ravager. Otherwise, it’s as the others described— Mr. Phainon’s current state appears to be caused primarily by repeated instances of severe emotional and mental stress, resulting in lasting trauma… Although I cannot say anything definitive without performing an actual tuning on him.”

“No, it’s too dangerous. If he was touched by a Lord Ravager, or bears the power of one within himself, then there’s a high possibility that the tuning will rebound and affect you, as it did with Miss Tingyun and Mr. Wonweek.”

“...That is certainly true.”

“For now, let’s try to find another way. Now that we have a clearer idea, we can narrow down our search.”

The unknown terms and names mean nothing to him. Mydei just knows that it’s not the answer he had been hoping for. But still, he holds his tongue, because he also knows that Phainon would never want to be healed at the expense of another person.

Their examination complete, Welt and Sunday finally step away from Phainon, turning back to Dan Heng and Mydei. Dan Heng, seeing that his companions are done, addresses them again. “What should we do next?”

Welt pauses, his eyes briefly falling on Mydei, who continues staring despondently at the unresponsive Phainon. Then, he places a hand on both Dan Heng’s and Sunday’s shoulders, gently pulling them aside. “Let’s touch bases with Stelle and the others first. I believe…we should allow Mr. Mydei some time alone with Mr. Phainon.”

Perhaps Mydei should reappraise this gentleman, if only for his tact. He makes a mental note of that for when he's in a better state of mind. In the meantime, Dan Heng and Sunday nod silently, allowing themselves to be guided away by Welt. As they walk away, Mydei hears traces of their conversation.

“Mr. Mydeimos and Mr. Phainon… Were they friends?”

“I think…they were a little more than that. So this might be quite hard on Mydei…”

“I’ve spoken briefly with the other Chrysos Heirs. It seems Mr. Phainon was very beloved among his companions. Most of them expressed similarly heartbroken sentiments upon learning about his condition…”

Mydei doesn’t hear the rest of what they say, but he neither wants nor needs to.

“My existence is of no consequence,” Phainon had once said. Mydei had not been close to him at the time and hadn’t bothered correcting him, but now he wishes he had. He wishes he could tell him now, show him that he matters, that he always did and always will, that he is and would always be an irreplaceable part of the Chrysos Heirs. And the indisputable proof of that is how much his fate had shaken all of them.

When he reaches over and cups Phainon’s cheek and receives no reaction, none of the receptiveness and gentle affections that he’d always get whenever he offered Phainon his tender touches, he feels the regret mounting.

Mydeimos the Undying scarcely bowed his head, rarely lowered himself onto his knees, and never, ever begged. And yet he finds himself doing all three things now, before the broken shell of his beloved, who is very much alive, and yet lacking all of the life that made him him.

Phainon is right in front of him, and yet he feels so unreachable that he may as well be dead.

“...Deliverer.”

He kneels, taking Phainon’s hands into his own. They’re warm, as they usually are, warmer than usual even, but they remain loose and limp in Mydei’s fingers.

“Deliverer.”

He presses his forehead to the backs of Phainon’s hands.

“Phainon.”

His voice grows quiet, so that he can conceal the tremor from the world, even if he can’t hide it from himself.

“...Please. Say something. Anything.”

Phainon doesn’t respond.

Chapter Notes

I wrote a majority of this chapter at 5 AM in the morning, after being woken up by a burst of inspiration as well as my cat. If you see any weird mistakes and typos, blame my cat

Barely a day passes before Anaxa gathers the Chrysos Heirs to discuss Phainon’s condition. Mydei and Aglaea are the first to show up at the allotted time and place, and the rest drift in closer to the agreed-upon hour. By the time the meeting commences, every Chrysos Heir has arrived—even the aloof Cipher, who remains in the shadow of a large pillar, watching and listening. Phainon himself is seated comfortably by the window, but his unseeing eyes remain fixed on one spot on the wall and unresponsive to any and all movements around him.

Anaxa clears his throat once the other Chrysos Heirs have settled into their places, commencing the meeting as if it were one of his lectures. “As you know, we have gathered today to discuss Phainon’s condition. I will cut right to the chase—after more thorough examination, Hyacine and I have been able to corroborate what the outlanders have told us. Some of Phainon’s current symptoms overlap with those exhibited by patients with severe traumatic brain injury. However… Because there were very few tangible causes, a complete recovery is highly unlikely, if not impossible, with existing treatment methods.”

“Physically, Lord Phainon is completely healthy,” Hyacine adds with a nod. “He’s even capable of standing and walking without support, and he’ll also chew and swallow if he’s given food or water.”

“Putting aside the fact that all of us, Phainon included, were restored with our status as demigods intact and have transcended beyond the need for most earthly necessities, we were able to confirm that, in some ways, Phainon actually fares better than most brain injury patients. And therein lies the current problem,” Anaxa sighs. “It is exceptionally difficult to treat

a wound that does not exist in the corporeal world. In typical cases, we would have to rely on therapy of the mind instead… But as you can see, that’s not possible either, as Phainon currently lacks the capability to perceive the world around him.”

“So?” Cipher asks from her corner. “What do you suggest we do, Grove boy? Because all I’m hearing is doom and gloom.”

“Do not interrupt me. I was just getting to that point." As he speaks, Anaxa slowly begins pacing from one end of the room to the other. “I posit two things. The first is that Phainon has suffered severe spiritual damage in addition to his brain damage, exacerbating the mental trauma he accumulated over 33,550,336 epochs. This is the main factor contributing to his current condition.”

He pauses, scanning the conference room and waiting for any questions or challenges to his statement. He doesn’t receive any—everyone is too demoralized by the assessment to say much of anything. Undeterred, Anaxa continues.

“The second… Is that while it will be incredibly difficult to reverse the damage, it’s not impossible, as long as we take the right approach.”

That prompts more of a reaction from those who have gathered. Mydei raises his head, but Aglaea is the one who speaks first, her tone terse.

“What are you proposing?”

“A multifaceted problem requires a multifaceted solution,” Anaxa explains matter-of-factly. “Rather than trying to treat an illness with no cure, we need only turn our focus to what can be healed—the soul. The rest of Phainon's recovery should follow naturally, allowing us to handle the other aspects of his condition using more conventional methods.”

“You speak as if the act of healing the soul is an easy feat,” Aglaea continues, her eyes narrowing. “One that does not require your blasphemous research and heretical experiments.”

“Ha…” Anaxa scoffs derisively. “I thought we were beyond these foolish debates. Answer me this, Lady Goldweaver. Are we really in any position to speak of blasphemy and heresy when everything we’ve ever known, including the pantheon that the people still cling so desperately to, has been turned upside down?”

The tension in the room reaches its head, palpable enough to cut through with a knife. Not a single person in the room dares to take a breath as the silent stand-off between Anaxa and Aglaea continues, though Tribbie fidgets, clearly wanting to intervene. Before she can, Aglaea crosses her arms, staring hard at Anaxa.

“Do forgive me for wanting to exercise due caution,” she says, her lips pursed. “But I simply dislike the idea of subjecting Phainon to more experimentation when he was…” She trails off, her fingers digging into her arms. “When he was already the primary target of Lycurgus’ cruel tests, and bore the consequences of them so that no one else had to.”

The room falls silent for the second time. Anaxa watches Aglaea with an unreadable expression, then sighs with a shake of his head.

“You really do have the lowest opinion of me,” he replies, maintaining an even tone. “I will obviously only use methods that are guaranteed to work. I’m not about to risk Phainon’s already fragile state with an experimental treatment.”

“Then can you assure everyone in this room right now that Phainon will be safe under your care?”

“Of course.” Anaxa allows for another brief pause before continuing, his voice softening. “He was one of my best students. Naturally, I would spare nothing but the best for him.”

Aglaea relaxes somewhat at that, letting her arms drop. “...Very well. If you can promise his safety, then you have my full support. Name the resources you require, and they will be provided.”

“...Oh? Now this is a surprise. Approving of my heretical methods is one thing, but you’ll be actively providing me with what I need? Have mountain goats started flying?”

“I’d advise you not to get used to this, Anaxagoras. These are outstanding circumstances. And I…” Aglaea turns, her gaze settling on Phainon. “I am willing to use any means necessary to ensure Phainon’s recovery.”

“Any means necessary…” Anaxa laughs through his nose, chewing on the statement. “I sincerely hope that it won’t have to come to that.”

The Chrysos Heirs disperse after that. Aglaea, Anaxa, and Hyacine reconvene to discuss their next course of action, while Cipher slips away without another word, with Tribbie following after her out of concern. Mydei lingers, intending to stay with Phainon until Anaxa returns, and he notices that Castorice hasn’t made to leave either. Instead of following the crowd, she had moved to stand beside Phainon instead, staring at him pensively. Seeing that she seems to be lost in thought, Mydei walks up to her.

“Castorice?”

“Oh…!” She starts a little, turning around to face Mydei. “Lord Mydei… You didn’t leave with the others?”

“No.” He doesn’t need to explain why. Castorice, the most staunch supporter of his and Phainons' relationship, immediately understands. “What are you still doing here?”

“Ah… Well…” She turns back to Phainon, who’s been still the entire time. “It was nice to see Lady Aglaea and Professor Anaxa talk at length without arguing… To see them putting aside their differences and working together,” Castorice says. “I was thinking, ‘Lord Phainon would be overjoyed.’ But when I saw him like this, I was struck with a powerful sense of loneliness… Surely, Lord Phainon must feel even lonelier than me right now, not being able to see or hear anything around him.”

Mydei looks down, trying to ignore the painful sting in his chest. He at least makes sure he doesn’t let it show on his face—after his long tenure as the crown prince of Castrum Kremnos, it’s second nature for him to appear strong and stoic. “...He does get lonely very easily,” he agrees. “Though he will rarely voice it.”

Dispirited by the confirmation, Castorice looks down, clutching her dress. “Lord Mydei… Do you think Lord Phainon would protest if he were to receive an embrace from me?”

Mydei raises his head, observing the young woman quietly. Castorice had her curse removed with her restoration, and she had wasted no time in showering her friends and comrades in all the affections she couldn’t give them before. However, she had been holding back with Phainon on the account that he would not be able to provide his consent. It’s an act of consideration befitting a sweet, mild-mannered girl like Castorice, but it is a little saddening to see that she still has so little confidence in herself as a person—especially when Phainon had treasured her friendship dearly.

“I don’t see why he would protest,” Mydei finally replies. “He always expressed remorse that he wasn’t able to do more to comfort you. I’m sure he would—” He falters for a split second. “I’m sure he would be happy to be embraced by you.”

Reassured, Castorice nods, then gingerly wraps her arms around Phainon’s shoulders. He remains completely still, not reacting at all, and her eyes glisten at the lack of response.

“...He’s warm. As warm as I imagined him to be,” Castorice whispers, pulling him a little closer. Unexpectedly, she continues speaking, perhaps spurred by her emotional state. “When he first arrived in Okhema, he was still so young. He was only as tall as my shoulder at first. Once, he referred to me as his ‘big sister’ by accident… He was so embarrassed about it, but that little accident warmed my heart and made me feel very happy…”

Her hold on him tightens still. “Ever since that day, I’ve always wanted to pat his head. Lord Mydei... Would he mind if I did it now?”

“...No,” Mydei says with certainty. “Not at all.”

Castorice nods again, then reaches up, gently tousling Phainon’s snow-white hair. Her lips curl into a soft but watery smile.

“He’s quite…fluffy,” she remarks, before hugging him once more. “One day… I hope to be able to do all of this when he is able to perceive these sensations.” She pauses. “Do you think that day will ever come, Lord Mydei…?”

She’s clearly looking for more reassurance, but Mydei has never been one to mince his words about chances and circumstances. The treatment that Anaxa had proposed is practically a shot in the dark, and even he hadn’t seemed completely sure that it would work. Mydei falls silent, mulling over how to respond, but he realizes quickly that there is only one answer.

They could not give up on Phainon. After all, Phainon had refused to give up on them—on the entire world—for 33,550,336 epochs.

“That day will come,” he replies resolutely. “Definitely.”

“...Mm.”

With that quiet agreement, Castorice nuzzles her face into Phainon’s hair, tears prickling at the corners of her eyes.

They remain like that in silence for a while longer, Castorice hugging Phainon, and Mydei standing silently by her side. Before long, the sound of footsteps breaks the silence, and both of them look up to see Hyacine approaching.

“Cassie. Lord Mydei.” She gives them both one of her smiles, though it’s more muted than usual. “I’m sorry… Was I interrupting anything?”

Castorice shakes her head, pulling away from Phainon. “No… Did Professor Anaxa or Lady Aglaea say anything about Lord Phainon?”

“They’re still discussing what to do next. Professor Anaxa said that he was thinking of contacting the Astral Express members before starting anything, since Dannie mentioned that there was someone on board who knew about mental healing, and another who knows a lot about memories.”

Mydei nods. The first one must be the wing-eared boy, Sunday. “I met one of them already. He came by to look at Phainon yesterday, but it seems like he wasn’t able to do much on his own.”

“Right… Dannie told us as much as well,” Hyacine says. “But we’re hoping that by combining the Nousporists’ research with the Astral Express’ capabilities, we’ll be able to make some progress. Lord Phainon’s condition is quite unique… So Professor Anaxa said we’ll need all the help we can get.”

“Is there anything we can do for Lord Phainon in the meantime?” Castorice asks hopefully.

“For now, Professor Anaxa told us to make him as comfortable as we can. That’s actually why I was here. Fresh air and movement will do Lord Phainon some good… And I thought we could take him to some of the places we’ve spent time together.” Her voice quivers slightly. “Just like our old days in the Grove.”

A melancholic look enters Castorice’s eyes. “...Yes. I agree. Perhaps bringing Lord Phainon to all of his favourite spots will trigger some of his memories, and bring him back to awareness.”

“That was my hope too.” Hyacine turns to Mydei, who has been hanging back quietly. “Lord Mydei… If you’re free, would you like to come with us?”

Mydei pauses, surprised he was considered at all. “I was never educated at the Grove. I have no place in your group.”

But Hyacine shakes her head. “That doesn’t matter. Lord Phainon really cherishes you… He always talks about you whenever he gets the chance to,” she says with a small laugh. “I’m sure he’d be happy if you were here too. But aside from that…

“Lord Mydei… You’ve been suffering too, haven’t you?”

Taken aback, Mydei is temporarily robbed of anything to say. But he also finds himself unable to deny how devastating this entire ordeal has been and looks away. How did she know? It’s a question that Mydei refuses to voice, but Hyacine smiles, answering him anyway.

“Even you can’t hide what your microexpressions give away, Lord Mydei,” she says knowingly. “I can see why Lord Phainon always referred to you as a kindred spirit or a soulmate… Beyond the similar experiences you share, you both have the same habit of swallowing your grief to appear strong in front of others…no matter how much you’re hurting on the inside.”

“...This shouldn’t be about me,” Mydei mutters. “It should be about Phainon.”

“I know… But that’s no reason why we should overlook our own pain. That’s why, I’ll ask again, Lord Mydei… Will you spend some time with the three of us, if you’re free?”

Mydei finally raises his head, looking first to Hyacine, who awaits his answer, then to Castorice, who watches him hopefully…then finally, to Phainon, who has been silent and unresponsive the entire time, unaware of the conversation they’re having.

Like this, Phainon seems like he can slip from Mydei's fingers so easily, and drift to a place where he will never be able to reach him.

He will not squander a single moment he could be spending with him. He refuses to.

Mydei brushes past Hyacine, approaching Phainon until he’s right in front of him.

“Deliverer—” He pauses. That false title feels like ash in his mouth now, after all the pain it has caused his beloved. “...Phainon. Let’s go.”

He gently takes one of his hands and pulls him to his feet. With his guidance, Phainon stands easily. It’s as Hyacine had said earlier—he doesn’t need to be supported, but from his lack of reaction, it’s obvious that he won’t be moving anywhere without being led.

“Lead the way,” Mydei says to Hyacine. She nods, walking ahead, with Castorice following closely behind. Mydei gently pulls Phainon along with him, squeezing his hand to assure him that he’s there.

Phainon doesn’t respond.

For the umpteenth time in a short week, an explosion rocks the depths of the Grove, shaking everything in the immediate area.

The golden threads shield Aglaea from the worst of it. Still, she’s left staring, unimpressed, as Anaxa stumbles out of the smoke, coughing and covered in singe marks from another failed experiment.

“I’m beginning to wonder whether you’re actually putting any effort into proving to me that your methods will work,” Aglaea says. “If so, you’ve done a spectacular job of convincing me otherwise.”

“How—how odd,” Anaxa retorts between wheezes. “There seems to be a —” He’s interrupted by another fit of coughing. “—a correlation between the success of my experiments and the presence of distractions currently in my lab.”

“Need I remind you who your current benefactor is? I don’t believe it is unreasonable for me to want some reassurance of your success.”

Finally recovering, Anaxa begins brushing the soot off his clothes. “Well, perhaps if you made yourself scarce, I would be able to focus more on perfecting my equations.”

“Enough, Anaxagoras. I know you’re using your own soul as the test subject of your experiments.”

Anaxa pauses in the middle of straightening out his tattered robes, then raises his head to regard Aglaea, his one eyebrow raised. “...Oh? And here I thought you would have had no understanding of the kind of work we carry out in the school of Nousporists.”

“I know enough on the matter of souls to understand what’s happening.” Aglaea narrows her eyes. “What you’re doing is incredibly risky.”

“I don’t suppose you’re about to suggest that I experiment on Phainon’s soul instead? Or worse, snatch an innocent bystander off the streets and turn them into my lab rat?” Anaxa crosses his arms. “Do you even have any right to be lecturing me when you had worn your own soul thin over the course of a thousand years?”

“...That was different.”

“It’s not different. Your hypocrisy aside, Phainon burned through his soul with hundreds of millions of coreflames, just so that we all could have a chance to live. It is only right, then, by the laws of equivalent exchange, that we are prepared to do the same for him.” He narrows his one eye, fixing Aglaea with a hard stare. “If you were in my position, you would be doing the same.”

Aglaea doesn’t deny it. She and Anaxa both know that she would. However, she doesn’t relent, crossing her arms and staring hard at him.

“And how do you think he would feel knowing that one of the very people he was fighting so hard to save had thoughtlessly thrown his life away?”

It’s Anaxa’s turn to fall silent. He stares at Aglaea, expression unreadable, allowing her words—her concern disguised behind the sharpened edge—to sink in, before laughing through his nose.

“Is that what this is about? Good grief… Might I suggest learning how to conduct yourself with some honesty?” He turns back to the ruined alchemic circle on the ground, crouching down to begin the process of reconstructing it. “Rest assured, my tests will have no lasting consequences on my own soul. It would defeat the purpose if I wore myself away before I was able to find a cure for Phainon, no?”

“...So long as you understand. By the way, I was wondering if you happened to see Cifera...” She pauses, then turns to the door, where two visitors are waiting. “You two have been standing there for a while. Speak.”

Castorice fidgets awkwardly, and Mydei remains silent behind her. He’s heard of Anaxa’s and Aglaea’s infamous disagreements from Phainon, and he wants no part in them, allowing Castorice to speak in his stead. “We were looking for Lord Phainon when we heard the explosion… Is everything alright?”

“Nothing to worry about,” Anaxa says with nonchalance unsuited to the scale of the “mishap.” “Phainon is with Hyacine right now. They were on the second floor the last time I saw them.”

Castorice nods, and the two quickly depart before Aglaea and Anaxa can begin arguing again.

It takes some searching, but Mydei and Castorice finally locate Phainon and Hyacine in one of the Grove’s many libraries. To their surprise, Dan Heng and Sunday are also with them; Dan Heng is sifting through various tomes and scrolls, while Sunday seems to be discussing something with Hyacine. Phainon is seated at a sunlit window with Little Ica resting on his lap, and if Mydei didn’t know any better, he would think that he’s simply basking in the sunlight.

Noticing Castorice’s and Mydei’s approach, Hyacine looks up from her conversation. “Oh! Cassie! Lord Mydei! You’re earlier than expected…”

“Are we interrupting?” Castorice asks meekly. “If you’re discussing something important, we can wait.”

“No, not at all. Me and Sunnie were just talking about possible treatment options for Lord Phainon.”

Sunday blinks, his ear wings twitching a little. “...Sunnie?”

Ignoring Sunday’s reaction, Mydei steps forward. “Have you made any progress?”

“Yes!” Hyacine says happily. She’s definitely in higher spirits than the last time Mydei saw her. “We were able to come up with some ways to combine traditional healing with Sunnie’s powers as a…” She pauses, glancing at Sunday for confirmation. “A Harmony Pathstrider, was it?”

“That’s correct, Miss Hyacine. Of course, whether these methods work or not remains to be seen,” Sunday adds. “We were advised by Mr. Anaxagoras to wait until he finalizes his work before we attempt anything on Mr. Phainon.”

Dan Heng walks over, some books tucked under his arms. “We also talked with Black Swan, a member of the Garden of Recollection. She said that for now, we should just focus on helping Phainon’s mind heal before doing anything related to his memories. Having him remember everything at once is likely to do him more harm than good,” he adds. “In an ideal scenario, he wouldn’t have suffered memory loss at all, but with this extent of brain damage, that’s highly unlikely…”

Mydei falls silent. The possibility that Phainon would have forgotten about him, about all of them, makes his gut churn. Castorice looks similarly downtrodden at the notion, and Hyacine, noticing the atmosphere has taken a turn for the worse, quickly intercedes.

“Anyway… I think that’s enough for today,” she announces. “Dannie, Sunnie, thank you so much for helping us.”

“Sorry I couldn’t do more. I’m…not much of a healer,” Dan Heng says, and Mydei swears he can detect a hint of bitterness in his expression. However, Hyacine quickly shakes her head.

“Not at all! You sifted through all those books so quickly, and you were able to find the information that we needed… It’s thanks to you that we were so productive today,” she says.

“I concur. Mr. Dan Heng truly lives up to his name as the Astral Express’ Archivist,” Sunday agrees with a nod.

Although Dan Heng doesn’t look entirely convinced, his expression is coloured by the faintest traces of bashfulness, and he apparently decides to let the topic drop. “Well, anyway… Are you going to take Phainon on another outing? Don’t let us keep you. Just go on ahead—me and Sunday will clean up and find our own way back.”

“Thank you so much!” With that, Hyacine trots over to Phainon and takes his hand, gently coaxing him onto his feet. Little Ica floats off, drifting lazily to Hyacine’s side. “Come on, Lord Phainon. The weather is quite nice today, so we’re going to go to one of our old hangouts.”

“Ah… You mean the place we used to study together?” Castorice pauses. “...Won’t that bring back bad memories of Professor Anaxa’s exams?”

“Maybe. But it’d be a start, right?” She smiles sadly. “I’m sure that after everything Lord Phainon’s been through, memories of exam season are probably least unpleasant of the ones he could relive.”

“...That’s true.”

Hyacine gently leads Phainon over to Mydei, looking up at him. “Would you like to do the honours, Lord Mydei?”

Mydei nods, and Hyacine lets go of Phainon’s hand, allowing him to take it instead. It’s still as warm as ever.

The place that Hyacine and Castorice lead him to is a quiet outdoor area veiled by a curtain of overhanging branches and leaves—the perfect place for anyone who wishes to further their academic pursuits uninterrupted, and certainly a location that Phainon would classify as a “secret hideout.” In normal circumstances, he would have cheerfully told Mydei as much, and Mydei would be mocking him for his infantile fantasies, and perhaps they’d get into an argument after that, which would eventually turn into some sort of competition.

Now, seated beside the abnormally silent Phainon and still holding his hand, Mydei can only yearn painfully for those carefree days.

“Is something on your mind, Lord Mydei?”

He raises his head to see Hyacine leaning close with a knowing smile on her face, though still far away enough so that she’s not intrusive. Little Ica is right behind her, staring at Mydei with their beady eyes. Mydei looks away.

“Nothing in particular,” he lies, and knowing that she’ll be able to see right through it, he asks, “Where’s Castorice?”

The two girls had been talking about something or another before Hyacine had come over. Mydei doesn’t know what about—he hadn’t exactly been paying attention—but either way, Castorice is nowhere to be seen now.

“She noticed some butterflies, so she wanted to follow them. I’m guessing she wants to take a picture of them,” Hyacine replies. “May I sit beside you, Lord Mydei?”

Mydei doesn’t answer, but shifts to allow her more room at the table. He’s practically pressed against Phainon now, but he doesn’t really mind. They have done far more intimate things at this point.

When would they be able to go back to those times, when he could embrace Phainon, kiss him, and hear the sound of his soft laughter as he received his tender affections in return?

Hyacine sits down, still leaving a small gap between herself and Mydei despite the limited room. She’s quite a petite girl, so she doesn’t take up that much space. As she makes herself comfortable, Little Ica flutters over to Phainon and sprawls themself across his head. “Thank you, Lord Mydei,” Hyacine says. “I’m happy you were able to make the time to come out with us today, seeing as you’ve been so busy.”

Mydei nods again, still quiet. Castorice and Hyacine had been arranging outings daily, but other than the first time, Mydei hadn’t been able to accompany them until today. Irontomb’s ravages had left much of Okhema in disrepair, but not wanting to risk the existence of the surviving people, the Astral Express and Genius Society had decided against attempting to restore the holy city to its former glory—a decision that Aglaea agreed with. She had reasoned that with the combined efforts of all the citizens, they would be able to rebuild their home manually, fostering more camaraderie between the people in the meantime—all while allowing their allies from beyond the sky to focus on the most heavily corrupted parts of their world.

The Kremnoans—the ones that had survived and had already been restored, anyway—had heralded the return of their king, immediately flocking to Mydei’s side, and he had recognized that in the chaos and tumult of Amphoreus’ ongoing restoration, his people once again needed a leader. He could not possibly foist that responsibility onto Aglaea when she already had her hands full overseeing both Okhema’s affairs and Phainon’s treatment. So as much as it pained him to leave Phainon’s side, he had placed his duties first, as always, making sure to direct his people as they aided with much-needed relief efforts around Amphoreus.

(When he asked, most of them had mentioned Phainon and how he had been helping them adjust to life in Okhema right up until the black tide struck the holy city. Mydei’s heart both warmed and ached at the notion that the swordsman had honoured his final request to him before they parted ways.)

Mydei is grateful, at least, that Castorice and Hyacine had been undeterred by his constant absences and continued extending their invitations to him. Other than remaining by Phainon’s side, there is little else he can do for him in this situation, and his utter powerlessness frustrates him.

“The scholar…” Mydei finds himself speaking. “Has he made any breakthroughs yet?”

Hyacine sighs softly. “Progress has been a little slow, but that’s to be expected. Professor Anaxa is tackling a very difficult task.” Sensing the Kremnoan’s anxiety, she looks up at him with a small but reassuring smile. “But if it’s one person who can succeed, it’s him. He’ll definitely pull through. The fact that we have assistance from beyond the sky is a huge help too, so let’s keep believing in him.”

“...Right.” Mydei casts a sidelong glance to Phainon, who has remained still and silent beside him, then smiles crookedly. “...Phainon never hesitated to sing praises about that man’s intelligence.”

“Hehe… When Lord Phainon was still studying at the Grove, he’d get into trouble with Professor Anaxa the most out of all the students in class.” Hyacine giggles at the memory. “But in spite of that, I could tell that the professor was very fond of him. He’s always fair during lectures, but he really favoured Lord Phainon and Cassie above everyone else… So he’s no doubt working especially hard to find a cure for Lord Phainon’s condition right now.”

“Mm…”

The two fall silent after that, content to wait until Castorice returns from her impromptu excursion. However, Mydei suddenly feels the hair-raising sensation of eyes on him, eyes on all of them. Immediately on high alert, he sits up straight, his eyes scanning the surroundings for any sign of an intruder. Startled, Hyacine looks up at him again.

“Lord Mydei? What’s wrong…?” Her eyebrows furrow. “You have quite a frightening look on your face…”

He doesn’t answer at first. He can’t determine whether the person watching them is doing so with good intentions or not, and he doesn’t want to frighten Hyacine if it’s a false alarm… But there is undeniably someone observing them, and it doesn’t sit right with him to let this continue unacknowledged.

Especially with Phainon in such a vulnerable state.

“...I just have to go verify something.” Letting go of Phainon’s hand for the first time, he stands. “Stay with Phainon. I’ll be back soon.”

It doesn’t take him long to locate the culprit. Hunting a lion is a fool’s errand; Mydei’s senses have been primed from the long years he has spent in the wilds of Amphoreus, and though his search brings him quite a distance away from their gathering, he still manages to pin down the exact position of his prey. Striding over to a cluster of branches, he gives the culprit no chance to slip away, thrusting his hand through the leaves without hesitation. His fingers close around what feels like the back of a hoodie, snatching the hunter-turned-prey and pulling them out of their hiding spot in an instant.

It’s only when he hears the yelp and sees the cat’s tail does he realize that he’s scruffed Cipher. His eyes widen as he observes her dangling limply from his grip.

“You…”

Nonplussed, Cipher crosses her arms, though she’s unable to convey the extent of her displeasure from her position. “Yeah, it’s me! Do you mind?”

At that, Mydei quickly puts her down, and she makes a big show of dusting herself off. “Sheesh… That’s more like it. Kids these days… They really don’t know how to respect their elders,” she sighs.

“...You were watching us,” Mydei states flatly.

“Does that offend you, little prince?”

“Did Aglaea send you?”

She rolls her eyes. “Why is that your first assumption? She and I aren’t joined at the hip, you know.”

As callous as Cipher’s words are, Mydei can detect something else behind them, though he can’t quite put a finger on what it is. However, he does recall that Aglaea had inquired about Cipher’s whereabouts a few days ago, expressing worry because she hadn’t been spotted around Okhema in that time. The realization strikes Mydei then.

“You’ve been watching over Phainon, Castorice, and Hyacine throughout their outings.”

Cipher stiffens ever so slightly. To any normal person, her change in demeanor would be imperceptible, but very few things can escape Mydei’s sharp eyes. Recovering quickly, the thief shrugs and asks again: “Does that offend you, little prince?”

“...No,” Mydei replies more softly. “I want to thank you for keeping an eye on Phainon while I couldn’t.”

“Hmm~? Aren’t you jumping the gun a little? How naive.” Cipher hums, turning around and wagging her finger at Mydei, a mischievous smile on her face. “What if I was just waiting for the perfect opportunity to snatch his wallet? He’d be easy pickings for any thief, you know. Completely unaware of his surroundings, wouldn’t even notice anything missing… Now that’s what I’d call a perfect target!”

“You’re not the kind of person who would take advantage of someone like that, despite what you say and how you present yourself.”

The smile fades from Cipher’s face, replaced by a slight scowl. Clicking her tongue, she straightens up and crosses her arms. “We’ve barely even talked, and you’re already acting like you’ve known me your entire life? I used to think that you were pretty awesome, what with your death-defying capabilities, but you’re actually kind of pretentious.”

“You’ve looked after the children of Castrum Kremnos before. The ones who were with the Kremnoan detachment.”

Cipher goes quiet. Mydei continues.

“Don’t bother denying it. The thief who would often play with the children when none of the adults were watching, who would lead them to the juiciest fruits and warn them of the black tide’s encroachment… Based on their descriptions, there’s no one it could have been other than you,” he says plainly. “It seems I owe you for more than just Phainon’s safety.”

The thief clicks her tongue for a second time, turning away. “Why don’t you put your money where your mouth is? If you’re talking about repayment, then you’d better be ready to fork up the cash, little prince. Words are cheap.”

“Very well. Name your reward, and it will be delivered to you.”

Surprised that Mydei had agreed so quickly, Cipher groans. “Ugh, never mind. Your straightforwardness took the fun out of it. I guess that’s why you and the Deliverer boy get along so swimmingly, huh?” She shrugs. “Oh well. If that’s all, I’m going.”

“Then allow me to thank you once again,” Mydei says before she can leave. “On both my behalf…and Phainon’s as well.”

Cipher doesn’t answer. And in the blink of an eye, she’s gone.

A few days pass, and regrettably, Mydei once again finds himself too occupied to join the outing that Hyacine and Castorice had arranged for the afternoon.

He knows he can't shirk his duties, but having to reject their invitation today feels a little worse than usual. His gut feeling keeps telling him that he should go with them—the two were planning to travel to the outskirts of Okhema with a caravan to help deliver supplies and provide aid to anyone in need, and while Hyacine had believed that a change of scenery would do Phainon some good as well, it doesn’t sit well with Mydei to let him go so far away without accompanying him.

Still… Castorice had also gone with them. Though she is now freed from her curse, her dominion over death remains the same. She is more than enough to protect Phainon, Hyacine, and the civilians they're traveling with in the worst case scenario. And if not, Hyacine had promised to text Mydei on the unlikely occasion that they ran into danger.

So why does the dread in his heart grow, not abating no matter how much menial labour he carries out alongside his people and Okhema’s citizens?

Try as he might to brush it aside, it lingers, persisting even as the hours drag on by, not dissipating even when he's given more tasks or when the Kremnoans come to him for guidance and request his leadership. But half the day passes uneventfully, with no news of anything happening from within or without the city, and he hasn't received any messages on his teleslate either. Hyacine and the others should be back within the hour, and that knowledge helps Mydei's mind settle a little.

Unfortunately, like always, his intuition rings true. While he's placing a pile of wooden beams down—more building materials needed for the many homes still in need of repair—the wind whips by him abruptly, and before he can write it off as an errant breeze, he sees Cipher in front of him, slightly out of breath. There’s a frantic look on her face that immediately strikes a strange sense of fear in Mydei’s heart.

“Bad news. The black tide struck where the Deliverer boy and the girls went,” she says breathlessly, not even bothering to conceal the fact that she had been tailing the group again. “There’re too many for me and Princess Homebody to handle on our own. We need help, and fast.”

Mydei feels his blood turn to ice in his veins.

The outworlders had warned the Chrysos Heirs of this risk already—the possibility that creatures of the black tide, remnants of Irontomb’s will, could still appear, and though they were lesser in number and could be vanquished permanently, they still posed very much of a threat to all lifeforms.

Hyacine had specifically chosen to embark on this excursion with Phainon because the area they had gone to was known to be safe from the black tide. She would never do something as irresponsible as endangering one of her patients.

This must have been some kind of freak accident that no one could have foreseen.

I should have gone with him.

That’s the only thought that occupies the god-king’s mind as he turns back to Cipher.

“Take me there,” he says urgently, for once uncaring of the fact that he’d be abandoning his post, but if there are lives on the line, surely the others would be understanding. Cipher doesn’t waste any time either, grabbing his arm with one hand and flipping her coin with the other. The journey is over in a fraction of a second, Okhema’s scenery morphing into a suburban landscape before Mydei can even draw breath.

He had once thought that the divine speed of Trickery would leave him feeling nauseated, but the trip had actually been smoother than he imagined. On the other hand, Cipher is clearly exhausted, doubled over with her hands on her knees as she gasps for breath. “Ugh… Sheesh… Has anyone ever told you how heavy you are?”

Mydei doesn’t answer, scanning the surroundings from the hillside Cipher has brought him to. The area is…eerily silent, not at all like the chaotic battlefield that Mydei had been envisioning. But as his head swivels around more, he spots corpses upon corpses of black tide beasts, he realizes that it’s because he’s not looking at a battle in progress, but the aftermath of a one-sided slaughter.

“Where’s Phainon?” he asks.

Cipher raises her head, staring up at him incredulously. “How am I supposed to know? He was down there with the others just now…”

Seeing no point in answering, Mydei quickly descends down the hillside, his heels raking through the grass and dirt as he allows gravity to carry him to the base. There’s still not a single sound that can tell him where Phainon and the others have gone, so he decides to follow the corpses of black tide beasts instead, not checking to see if Cipher is behind him. Eventually, Hyacine comes into view, along with Little Ica and the civilians huddled around her, and Mydei wastes no time in running over.

“Hyacine.” He announces his presence with the call, his calm tone belying the growing franticness he feels. Having been in the middle of healing an injured man, Hyacine's head snaps up, her eyes widening with both shock and relief when she sees Mydei kneeling down beside her.

“Lord Mydei…” Her eyes flick to a spot behind him. Cipher must have finally caught up with him. “Lady Cipher…” She sounds a little shaken, but a quick glance-over tells Mydei that she’s completely unharmed. That’s a good sign. “How did you two…?”

“Never mind that. What happened?” Mydei asks.

“The black tide began surging out of nowhere all of a sudden…” From the look on Hyacine’s face, she seems to be torn by guilt. “I don’t know what could have caused it. There were never any reports of its encroachment near this area…”

“It’s not your fault,” Mydei quickly says to reassure her. “No one could have predicted this would happen.” He pauses, his eyes traveling over the group that has gathered around Hyacine. Phainon and Castorice tend to stand out, and the fact that he spotted neither of them immediately tells him all he needs to know. “Where are Phainon and Castorice?”

“Cassie is scouting the area just in case there are more black tide monsters. As for Lord Phainon, he’s…”

Hyacine raises her head, looking off into the distance. Mydei follows her gaze to a scene of absolute carnage, where even more black tide beasts lie dead, some intact, others hacked to pieces, and others still mutilated until they are barely recognizable.

And at the epicenter of it all is Phainon.

Unharmed but completely still, he’s not facing the group, but he seems to be staring blankly ahead, his clothes flowing listlessly in the light breeze. Dawnmaker is still in his hand, nearly slipping from his loosening grip.

Mydei doesn’t know what to make of the scene.

“...Phainon?” he whispers. “Why is he…”

Before Hyacine can say anything, the man she is healing raises his head. “Lord Phainon… As soon as the black tide beasts drew closer to him, he suddenly leapt into action,” he says, his eyes shining with awe. “It was incredible! He tore through their ranks so quickly, as if it was as easy as breathing! He may have fallen still now, but the way he moved before... It was as if a silver storm had descended upon the enemies! His strength and skill are the stuff of legends!” The man’s voice quivers as he finishes recounting the tale, a gleeful smile spreading across his face.

“No matter what, his heroic spirit lives on! He really is Amphoreus’ Deliverer!”

That declaration stings more than Mydei realizes is possible. Perhaps it's because it's uttered without consideration for what that heroism had cost Phainon.

The man must know of Phainon’s condition. Most Okhemans do—it would've been impossible to hide it, when he had been so involved around the city, had charmed and befriended virtually every citizen with his sunny smiles and his willingness to drop everything to help anyone in need. But none of them then would never truly know about the horrors he has been through—the way that Lygus had toyed with him like a lab rat, until his body had been reduced to charcoal and bone and his mind had but a single shred of sanity left to cling to, sustained only by equal parts hatred and love.

They will never really know the truth behind Phainon’s current state.

“Intra-Cognition is null. Responds only to destructive stimuli.”

Mydei remembers the words as clear as day, and he knows immediately that Phainon had only responded to the threat because it's muscle memory for him to meet destruction with destruction.

There is nothing left of him but that primal instinct—all the other parts of him had long been shaved away by the millions of iterations of his past selves and the heat of the coreflames that had consumed him for an equal amount of epochs.

That realization is almost as devastating as if Phainon had simply fallen to the beasts in his vulnerability.

Silently, Mydei stands up and begins walking over. Though Phainon doesn’t move, there’s a part of him that fears that he will vanish right before his eyes, and the unwanted thought prompts him to quicken the pace. Luckily, no such thing happens, and Phainon remains where he is until Mydei circles around him to face him. His blue eyes are still dull and unfocused, staring right through him, and his expression is blank. Nothing has changed.

“...Phainon.”

Mydei slowly wraps his arms around Phainon, pulling his head into his shoulder and holding him there gently.

“They’re all gone now,” Mydei murmurs into his hair. “Let’s go home.”

Phainon doesn’t respond.

Chapter End Notes
